subModules.title: Reading Mission: Non-defining Relative Clauses: Adding Insightful Commentary & Context

content.summary: In this reading module, you will explore how professional writers add extra details and interesting facts to their stories using non-defining relative clauses. By paying attention to commas and relative pronouns such as who, which, and whose, you will learn how to make your reading comprehension sharper and your understanding of complex sentences much clearer.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Non-defining relative clauses using who, which, and whose, separated by commas.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Professional terms related to offices, management, documents, and business projects.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming for general context and scanning for supplementary details embedded within commas.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of professional texts containing descriptive extra information.
Locate specific facts tucked inside non-defining relative clauses.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns involving commas and relative pronouns.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you read an article about a successful company, what kind of extra information do you find most helpful?
options: Extra details about the history and location of the office
Random gossip about the employees' personal lives
Unrelated weather forecasts from different cities
contextWarmup.explanation: Articles about companies often include extra background facts, such as office locations and history, to give readers a complete and professional picture.

rules: Gunakan koma sebelum dan sesudah clause: Subject, who/which/whose + verb..., main verb. Contoh: My brother, who lives in Singapore, visits us twice a year.
Jangan gunakan 'that' dalam non-defining clauses. Gunakan 'who' untuk orang, 'which' untuk benda/hewan, 'whose' untuk kepemilikan. Contoh: The laptop, which I bought last month, works perfectly.

Informasi dalam clause bisa dihilangkan tanpa mengubah makna inti kalimat. Contoh: Dr. Sarah, who graduated from Oxford, is our new lecturer. (Tanpa clause: Dr. Sarah is our new lecturer - masih jelas siapa yang dimaksud).
Dalam bahasa lisan, tandai dengan jeda pendek atau intonasi menurun saat membaca clause ini. Contoh tertulis: The meeting, which lasted three hours, was very productive.

commonTrap.explanation: Many learners incorrectly use the word 'that' in non-defining relative clauses, or they forget to include the commas that separate the extra information from the main sentence.
commonTrap.wrong: The office building, that was built last year, has solar panels.
commonTrap.correct: The office building, which was built last year, has solar panels.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Non-defining Relative Clauses for Richer Context

content.summary: Learn how to use non-defining relative clauses to add extra commentary and context to your writing. This structure helps you provide interesting details about people, places, and things without changing the main message of your sentence.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Identify the Main Clause and Extra Information
blueprintItems.formula: Main Subject + Extra Information Clause + Main Verb + Object / Complement
blueprintItems.example: My brother, who lives in Singapore, visits us twice a year.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Choose the Correct Pronoun (Who, Which, Whose)
blueprintItems.example: The old library, which contains thousands of rare books, closes on Sundays.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Check Punctuation and Sentence Flow
blueprintItems.formula: Noun phrase + Comma + relative clause + Comma + rest of sentence
blueprintItems.example: Dr. Sarah, who graduated from Oxford, is our new lecturer.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use commas before and after a non-defining relative clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: My car which I bought last year breaks down often.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: My car, which I bought last year, breaks down often.
mechanicsRules.why: Commas show that the information inside is extra and not strictly necessary to identify the noun.

mechanicsRules.rule: Never use the word 'that' in a non-defining relative clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Mr. Harrison, that teaches history, is very patient.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Mr. Harrison, who teaches history, is very patient.
mechanicsRules.why: English grammar rules forbid 'that' in non-defining clauses. Use 'who' for people and 'which' for things.

mechanicsRules.rule: Ensure the main sentence still makes complete sense if you remove the clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The concert was amazing which we attended last night.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The concert, which we attended last night, was amazing.
mechanicsRules.why: The extra information sits inside commas right after the noun it describes.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Non-defining Relative Clauses: Adding Insightful Commentary & Context

content.summary: This speaking lab focuses on using non-defining relative clauses smoothly in spoken English. When speaking, you must use slight pauses around the relative clause, which acts as extra commentary. Your voice should drop slightly in pitch during the clause and rise back to normal when you return to the main sentence.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to comma intonation. In writing, we use commas. In speech, we use micro-pauses before and after words like who, which, where, and whose to signal extra information without breaking the flow of your speech.

pillars.name: Micro-pauses for Commas
pillars.target: Brief pauses before and after relative clauses
pillars.explanation: Native speakers signal non-defining relative clauses in speech by inserting a very short pause before the relative pronoun and another pause at the end of the clause.

pillars.name: Pitch Drop on Parenthetical Information
pillars.target: Slight lowering of pitch for extra commentary
pillars.explanation: When you add extra commentary using a non-defining clause, lower your pitch slightly so the listener knows this is extra information rather than the main point.

pillars.name: Relative Pronoun Clarity
pillars.target: Clear articulation of who, which, whose, where
pillars.explanation: Do not swallow relative pronouns. Pronounce 'who' clearly as /huː/, 'which' as /wɪtʃ/, and 'whose' as /huːz/ to maintain grammatical clarity.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using a non-defining relative clause with 'who':
practicumQuestions.promptText: My grandfather is eighty years old. He still runs every morning.
practicumQuestions.hint: Put the extra information about your grandfather inside commas.
targetAnswers: My grandfather, who is eighty years old, still runs every morning.
My grandfather, who is 80 years old, still runs every morning.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use commas before and after 'who is eighty years old' to insert the commentary.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and grammar in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: our car which we bought last year broke down yesterday.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check capitalization at the start and add commas around the clause.
targetAnswers: Our car, which we bought last year, broke down yesterday.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Capitalize 'Our', place a comma after 'car', and place another comma after 'year'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct relative pronoun (who, which, or whose):
practicumQuestions.promptText: The smartphone, ______ I bought online, stopped working after a week.
practicumQuestions.hint: The noun before the blank is a smartphone (an object).
targetAnswers: which
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'which' for things and objects in non-defining relative clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a non-defining relative clause with 'whose':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The artist won the national prize. Her paintings are inspired by nature.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'Her' with 'whose' to show possession.
targetAnswers: The artist, whose paintings are inspired by nature, won the national prize.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Whose' connects the artist to her paintings, showing possession inside commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Identify why this sentence is incorrect and provide the corrected version:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The hotel that we stayed at in Rome was extremely comfortable.
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember the rule about 'that' in non-defining clauses.
targetAnswers: The hotel, which we stayed at in Rome, was extremely comfortable.
The hotel, which we stayed at, was extremely comfortable.
practicumQuestions.explanation: You cannot use 'that' in non-defining clauses. Use 'which' with commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a sentence about your English teacher using a non-defining relative clause with 'who':
practicumQuestions.promptText: My English teacher / patient / explains grammar clearly
practicumQuestions.hint: Example pattern: My teacher, who is very patient, explains grammar clearly.
targetAnswers: My English teacher, who is patient, explains grammar clearly.
My English teacher, who is very patient, explains grammar clearly.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The clause 'who is patient' adds extra commentary about the teacher between commas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join these ideas into one sentence using a non-defining relative clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Mount Bromo is located in East Java. It attracts many landscape photographers.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'which' for Mount Bromo.
targetAnswers: Mount Bromo, which is located in East Java, attracts many landscape photographers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Insert the location detail between commas using 'which'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Add the missing commas to complete this non-defining relative clause sentence correctly:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Dr. Henderson who has written three books on history will lecture tonight.
practicumQuestions.hint: Commas surround the extra description of Dr. Henderson.
targetAnswers: Dr. Henderson, who has written three books on history, will lecture tonight.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A comma is required before 'who' and after 'history'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with an appropriate non-defining clause about a laptop:
practicumQuestions.promptText: My new computer, _____________, is fast and lightweight.
practicumQuestions.hint: Add a detail about its screen, weight, or purchase time using 'which'.
targetAnswers: My new computer, which I bought last week, is fast and lightweight.
My new computer, which has a large screen, is fast and lightweight.
My new computer, which cost a lot of money, is fast and lightweight.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Any logical clause starting with 'which' and enclosed in commas works here.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence describing your favorite book using a non-defining relative clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: My favorite book / fascinating plot / keeps me awake at night

targetAnswers: My favorite book, which has a fascinating plot, keeps me awake at night.
My favorite book, which features a fascinating plot, keeps me awake at night.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A well-formed non-defining clause uses 'which', appropriate commas, and adds insightful context.
